analysis.one_liner: Extends federal-employee-style comprehensive health insurance to all Americans, funded by employer payroll taxes.
analysis.headline: The bill never advanced past committee referral and died when the 110th Congress ended in January 2009, without a single committee or floor vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have created an American Health Benefits Program covering everyone not already insured through Medicare, Medicaid, VA, or an employer, run like the Federal Employees Health Benefits Program that covers Members of Congress. Private insurers would bid to offer plans under federal rules: community-rated premiums, no pre-existing condition exclusions, and at least 90 percent of premiums spent on actual care. The government would pay up to 75 percent of premiums, with extra subsidies for lower-income families, funded by a new excise tax on employers of roughly 4 to 10 percent of wages, a parallel tax on self-employment income, and a 2 percent tax on hospital revenues. It was referred to two House committees and never received a hearing, vote, or further action before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: The roughly 46.5 million uninsured Americans — over 80 percent of them workers or their dependents — would gain comprehensive coverage identical in scope to what federal employees get, with government contributions of up to 75 percent of premiums and full premium and cost-sharing subsidies for the lowest-income families. Families between the poverty line and twice the poverty line would get sliding-scale subsidies, with children and pregnant women at those incomes paying nothing out of pocket. People with pre-existing conditions could no longer be excluded or charged more.

how_it_helps.text: Every American not already covered by Medicare, Medicaid, TRICARE, VA, or comparable employer insurance would be enrolled in a qualified health plan providing the same comprehensive benefits package that Members of Congress and federal employees receive, with no exclusions for pre-existing conditions and premiums that cannot vary by age, gender, or health status [S2] [S3].

The federal government would contribute up to 75 percent of the premium, following the same formula used for federal employees' coverage, and low-income families at or below roughly twice the poverty line would get subsidies reducing or eliminating premiums and cost-sharing; children and pregnant women at those incomes would pay nothing out of pocket [S3].

Plans would have to return at least 90 percent of premiums as actual health care benefits, participate in a shared high-risk reinsurance pool, and meet consumer protections based on FEHBP standards [S3].

The bill's findings cited 46.5 million uninsured Americans in 2006, over 80 percent of them workers or their dependents, and $41 billion in uncompensated care that shifted costs onto everyone else [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Employers would pay a new excise tax of 4 to 10 percent of wages (credited when they provide equivalent coverage themselves), the self-employed a parallel tax on their income, and hospital-owning corporations a 2 percent tax on hospital revenues. Individuals required to enroll would owe premiums, collected through paycheck withholding, though the government would pick up most of the cost.

drawbacks.text: Every employer would owe a new payroll tax of roughly 4 to 10 percent of wages, with the highest rates falling on firms whose workers earn the most, and the self-employed would owe a parallel tax on their income [S3].

The bill included an individual mandate: every eligible person had to enroll in a qualified plan or be auto-assigned to the cheapest basic plan in their region, with premiums collected through tax withholding [S3].

Corporations operating hospitals would pay a new 2 percent tax on hospital revenues, and federal payments to hospitals serving uninsured Medicaid patients would be phased down to 10 percent of 2010 levels over five years [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit was large and universal: everyone without employer or public coverage would get comprehensive insurance modeled on the plan Members of Congress get, with no pre-existing condition exclusions and zero cost-sharing for the poorest families, children, and pregnant women [S3]. The cost was also large and spread across employers, the self-employed, and hospitals, and the bill left in place a system where private insurers remain the permanent channel for coverage, regulated but entrenched. The bill never received a committee vote, so none of this was ever weighed on the record.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Ways and Means and Energy and Commerce committees and then to a Health Subcommittee, and no committee ever took it up before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. James Langevin introduced the bill on February 12, 2008, joined by one Republican cosponsor, Rep. Christopher Shays [S1] [S4].
The House referred it to the Ways and Means Committee and the Energy and Commerce Committee the same day, and it was then referred to the Subcommittee on Health [S5].
No markup, vote, or further action followed, and the bill expired when the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009 [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The 46.5 million uninsured gained nothing, and the status quo held: employers and the self-employed never faced the new payroll tax, hospitals never faced the revenue tax, and insurers kept the existing market without community-rating or guaranteed-issue requirements.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The uninsured remained uncovered; the status quo held

sides.party_line_note: The bill had just one Democratic sponsor and one Republican cosponsor and never drew a floor vote, so no partisan split was ever recorded.

industries.note: Coverage would be delivered entirely through private insurers contracting with a new federal administrator, much as FEHBP does today — guaranteed customer base for the industry, in exchange for community rating, a 90 percent medical-benefit requirement, and a ban on pre-existing condition exclusions.

Employers would owe a new excise tax of roughly 4 to 10 percent of wages, credited back for any period an employee has equivalent employer coverage — so firms already providing good coverage would largely offset the tax, while those not providing it would pay in full.

A new 2 percent tax on hospital revenues, but the bill cited $41 billion a year in uncompensated care for the uninsured that universal coverage would largely eliminate; Medicaid disproportionate-share payments would phase down to 10 percent over five years.
Self-employment income would be subject to the same percentage tax as employer payrolls, though credited for months covered by equivalent employer-provided insurance.
